The suit was contested by defendant No.2, who is the present petitioner, by filing written statement stating that the allegations made in the plaint are false, there is no cause of action, the suit is not maintainable, the suit is barred by limitation. It was further asserted that it was an out and out sale, there was no agreement for reconveyance, the said agreement has been created by ante-dating and, as a matter of fact, defendant Nos. 1 and 2 are near relations of the plaintiff and defendant Nos. 1 and 2 entrusted the plaintiff to auction purchase the suit property and the plaintiff fraudulently auction purchased the same in his own name and finally, at the intervention of the arbitrators he executed the kabala and delivered possession and thereupon, the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 transferred the same to defendant No. 3 and delivered possession who mutated the Khatian in his name within the knowledge of the plaintiff and the plaintiff earlier filed an application for redemption where defendant No. 1 appeared and challenged the agreements to be forged and the plaintiff did not proceed with the same. 

 7. Dr Rafiqur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite party, opposes the Rule and submits that the Court never found the agreement in question "ante-dated" as argued by the learned Lawyer for the petitioner rather, the trial Court has observed that the stamp of agreement is a 5 months prior purchase from the date of execution on 19-7-96 and no explanation or reason has been shown in pleadings and arguments of plaintiff to that effect and ante-date means to affix with a date earlier than the true date and it is very much in the record that date of execution of the kabala deed and the agreement of reconveyance was on 19-7-69 but the stamps for the agreement was purchased 5 months earlier on 5-4-69 and there is no illegality to use any stamp previously purchased for another purpose and thus the finding of the trial Court to that effect is not based on law or reasoning. He next submits that the appellate Court has reversed the findings of the trial Court on all points and has categorically observed that the Assistant Judge, the trial Court, has misconceived and misconstrued the facts of the suit. The learned Lawyer also submits that the agreement was duly proved and it was filed before the trial Court and it is not the requirement of law that the scribe of any document should come before the Court to prove it The learned Lawyer submits that the original agreement was found to be missing from the Court record and when it was detected by the lower appellate Court that the exhibit list has not been prepared, signed and sealed and exhibits were not marked, the lower appellate Court step back the record to the trial Court to have the exhibits marked and to prepare the list and to sign and seal it and this omission is nothing but technical irregularities and justice cannot be defeated for mere omission or technical irregularity. The learned Lawyer also submits that the defendant No.3 filed an application before the lower appellate Court for vacating the order dated 19-10-94 passed by the Court sending back the record to the trial Court to have the exhibit list prepared, signed, sealed and marked. The said application of the defendant No.3 was rejected by the order dated 14-1-95 against which defendant No.3, the present petitioner, did not file any application before this Court under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and also did not raise any objection before the trial Court at the time of preparation of the list The learned Lawyer emphasises that the agreement in question is not a simple contract but an agreement for reconveyance which as per section 95(A) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act made the transfer of land of the plaintiff to defendant Nos. 1 and 2 nothing but a complete usufructuary mortgage which created a legal right automatically in favour of the plaintiff to get back his land after 3 years and so the claim of defendant Ned as bonafide purchaser for value without notice of the agreement under section 27(b) of the Specific Relief Act is not applicable. He also submits that agreement of reconveyance can be specifically enforced and provision of registration is not applicable and even oral agreement proved by sufficient evidence may be specifically enforced by the transferor. He next submits that the lower appellate Court found that all the PWs corroborated each other as to the execution of the deed of agreement and the lower appellate Court also found the agreement as a genuine document and not a forged one. He next submits that though the defendant pleaded a case of fraud and collusion, he did riot lead any evidence to prove the same. Lastly, the learned Lawyer for the opposite party submits that the lower appellate Court has rightly allowed the appeal following all the provisions of law which may not be interfered by this Court in its jurisdiction under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

 8. I have perused the revisional application along with the judgments of the Courts below and the materials on record and heard the learned lawyers appearing on behalf of the petitioner and the opposite parties. It appears that the trial Court found the agreement in question to be a forged one. The defendant pleaded a case of fraud and forgery which was not proved by evidence. In cases of fraud, collusion or undue influence the onus is on the party who alleges it as such to prove the allegation. There is a presumption of good faith on human transaction as there is a presumption of innocence in criminal matter and, that being so, the burden of proving every species of bad faith such as fraud, collusion, forgery, etc, rushes on the person who asserts the same. The lower appellate Court believed the document to be genuine and has observed, that the trial Court has misconceived and misconstrued the facts of the suit. It further appears that the plaintiff filed the original copy of the agreement before the trial Court on 11-4-81 with the attached list and on 27-2-83 he filed an application before the trial Court for getting back the original copy of the agreement and the said application was allowed by the order dated 27-2-83 and he took back the original copy of the same. On 22-9-84 he filed the said original copy of the agreement again with a firstly but due to inadvertence there is no record of it in the order sheet and when the deed was found to be missing he brought it to the notice of the Court by an application dated 30-12-84 but there was no order on that application. The trial Court allowed the use of the photocopy of the original agreement on evidence. It appears that the trial Court was fully satisfied about the whereabouts of the original copy of the agreement and its execution and it was marked as Exhibit-I by the trial Court as per the order of the appellate Court correcting its own omission. The appellate Court found that all the documents are in the record but the exhibit list has not been prepared, signed, sealed and exhibits were not marked and by the order dated 19-10-94 the lower appellate Court sent the record to the trial Court to have the exhibit list prepared, signed, sealed and marked and the trial Court corrected the omission. Rules or procedures are made to subserve the ends of justice and not to defeat them. Mere omission to sign and seal exhibits or deposition sheets does not affect the merit of the case nor the jurisdiction of the Court and such omissions are mere defects or irregularities in the procedure and not an illegality when section 99 of the Code of Civil Procedure aims to prevent such procedural technicalities. Non compliance of the procedure for marking the exhibits and to prepare the exhibits list does not destroy the validity of the Court proceeding. It appears that the plaintiff has discharged the primary onus to prove the genuineness of the disputed agreement. The Court may at any stage of the suit reject any document which it considers irrelevant or inadmissible after recording the grounds. No plea was taken in the Courts below about the admissibility of the document which was proved by PW s 1, 2 and 3. The trial Court failed to appreciate how to prove a document as per section 73 of the Evidence Act and what constitutes forgery of a document under sections 463 and 464 of the Penal Code. The defendant No. 1 in his written statement only alleged that the document is forged and created but did not prove such allegation by adducing evidence during trial. Though the defendant pleaded a case of fraud and forgery he did not lead any evidence to preve the same and mere statement in the written statement is not enough nor it is an evidence by itself unless such statement is proved by leading evidence by its maker. It is now a settled principle of law that unless objection as to admissibility of a document was taken at the earlier opportunity i.e. at the time of admitting the document into evidence, the question of its admissibility cannot be raised at a subsequent stage. Although the date of execution of both the safkabala deed and the agreement of reconveyance was on 19-7-69 but the stamp of agreement was purchased earlier and there is no illegality in purchasing the stamp. On the permission of the trial Court the photocopy was used during taking of evidence before the trial Court and after being fully satisfied it was treated as exhibit-1 by the trial Court. The lower appellate Court disbelieved the case of the defendant No.3.
